steps.title: Two families of prefix
steps.html:
A prefix is a piece added to the front of a word that changes its meaning without changing its class. Legal and illegal are both adjectives; understand and misunderstand are both verbs. That is why prefixes are worth learning: once you know the piece, you can read a word you have never met.

The number family tells you how many: mono- one, bi- two, semi- half, multi- many, inter- between. The negative family tells you that something is not the case (il-, im-, ir-, in-, un-), is the opposite or a refusal (dis-), or has been done wrongly (mis-).

steps.title: Choosing between the negatives
steps.html:
• in- is the basic form, but it changes to fit the word: il- before l (illegal, illogical), im- before m and p (immature, impossible), ir- before r (irresponsible, irregular).
  • un- is the everyday alternative and attaches to almost anything: unhappy, unimaginative. Where both exist, they are rarely interchangeable: unable, not inable.
  • dis- reverses or refuses: disapprove is to think something is wrong, not to approve badly.
  • mis- is the only one that means wrongly: misunderstand, mishear, mislead.

steps.title: Text A · The morning thread
steps.html:
Written for this course. Messages between three museum volunteers.

Priya, 08.14 — Been here since eight. Nothing in the hall yet. Banners still in boxes. Multicoloured ones for the courtyard, plain for inside — don’t mix them up.

Dan, 08.31 — On my way. Stuck on the ring road. Any sign of the bilingual signs? Ordered them in March, never came. Rang twice. No answer either time.

Priya, 08.33 — Arrived Friday. In the office, under the box of programmes. Sam’s doing the chairs — semicircle in front of the monoplane, not rows. Looks better and holds more.

Sam, 09.02 — Morning both. Chairs done. Two rooms interconnect now the builders have gone, so people can walk straight through instead of going back round. Much better for the tour.

Priya, 09.10 — Good. Programmes here too. Two hundred years of this place, and the first batch came back with the date wrong. Reprinting. Cost me an afternoon.

Sam, 09.14 — How many wrong? All of them, or just the first box?

Dan, 09.40 — Here at last. Parked behind the delivery bay. Illegal, I know. Ten minutes, no more.

Priya, 09.44 — Move it. Warden was round twice yesterday. Fined one of the caterers’ drivers. Forty pounds, apparently.

Dan, 10.31 — Catering confirmed. Sixty for the reception, forty for the talk. Tea urns from the church again. Ours still broken since March.

Priya, 10.36 — Fine. Guest book on the desk by the door, not by the monoplane. People stop to write and block the doorway.

Sam, 10.15 — Question. The figurehead — the semi-human one from the wreck — hall or side room? Was in the hall last time. Bit dark in there now, though.

Priya, 10.18 — Hall. Everyone photographs it. Side room’s for the biannual newsletter display and the old photographs. Lights fixed on Monday anyway.

steps.title: Text B · Midday, and the note on the door
steps.html:
Written for this course. The same thread later, a note pinned to a door, and an email.

Dan, 11.02 — Bad news. Speaker’s flight delayed. Intercontinental, so nothing before tomorrow evening now. Not tonight.

Sam, 11.05 — Which speaker? The semi-retired professor, or the one who pays for everything?

Dan, 11.07 — The professor. The multimillionaire’s driving up. Arrives Thursday, wants an hour in the hall first.

Priya, 11.12 — Fine. Professor first, donor second. Keep the professor short — lovely man, but speaks in a monotone and nobody lasts twenty minutes.

Priya, 11.31 — One more thing. Donor wants a photograph with the monoplane. Not with the sandwiches. Make sure somebody’s watching.

Sam, 11.20 — Ladder found. Behind the boiler, of course. Bulbs next.

Dan, 15.02 — Van driver rang back. Six banners still in the depot. Says Thursday morning. Chasing him again at eight.

Sam, 17.12 — Bulbs done, side room usable. Left the ladder by the stairs. Someone move it before Thursday, please.

Priya, 17.44 — Programmes reprinted, correct date, bicentenary logo on the cover. Two boxes in the office, one in the hall. Don’t open the hall box till Thursday morning, and keep it away from the caterers.

Pinned to the office door, 16.40 — Gone to the printer’s. Back by six. Banners counted — forty-two. Should be forty-eight. Six missing, probably still in the van, unless the driver unloaded them somewhere else. Don’t move the chairs. P.

Email, 21.55. From Priya. Subject: Bicentenary, Thursday — Dan, Sam — quick summary before I forget. Signs: found, in the office. Chairs: done, semicircle, please leave them. Figurehead: hall, not side room. Speaker: delayed, so Thursday not Wednesday. Banners: six short, chasing the driver in the morning. Anything I’ve missed, tell me tonight rather than at eight on Thursday. P.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
Courtyard shut. Everyone through folklore. Signs up but half wrong — ignore the two by the stairs, fixing them at twelve. Halloran 11.50, ten minutes, before the film. Told him myself, still speaking to me. Grass illegal this year. Tickets from nine, two already. Anything else, ring me. Not before eleven.

Model 2 · the public notice

Welcome to our bicentenary weekend.

The courtyard entrance is closed today. Visitors should enter through the folklore gallery, where the two rooms now interconnect; families with young children may prefer to be warned about the semi-human figures on the left. Our bilingual signs are in place, although a small number are being corrected during the morning, and staff in multicoloured badges will be happy to direct you.

Mr Halloran, whose gift built this wing, will speak at 11.50, immediately before the intercontinental flight film at twelve. Seating is arranged in a semicircle in front of the monoplane.

Please note that parking on the grass is illegal this year and tickets are being issued.
